source_text: Qualis est autem tortuositas vestra, ut ipsam EX syllabam praepositionis officio adscriptam auferre quaeratis, et alia magis uti, quae in hac specie non invenitur penes scripturas sanctas? Per virginem dicitis natum, non ex virgine, et in vulva, non ex vulva, quia et angelus in somnis ad Ioseph: Nam quod in ea natum est, inquit, de spiritu sancto est, non dixit ex ea. Nempe tamen, etsi ex ea dixisset, in ea dixerat; in ea enim erat quod ex ea erat. Tantundem ergo et cum dicit in ea et ex ea consonat, quia ex ea erat quod in ea erat. Sed bene quod idem dicit Matthaeus, originem domini decurrens ab Abraham usque ad Mariam, Iacob, inquit, generavit Ioseph, virum Mariae, ex qua nascitur Christus. Sed et Paulus grammaticis istis silentium imponit. Misit, inquit, deus filium suum factum ex muliere. Numquid per mulierem, aut in muliere? Hoc quidem impressius, quod factum potius dicit quam natum; simplicius enim enuntiasset natum. Factum autem dicendo et, Verbum caro factum est, consignavit, et carnis veritatem ex virgine factae adseveravit. Nobis quoque ad hanc speciem psalmi patrocinabuntur, non quidem apostatae et haeretici et Platonici Valentini, sed sanctissimi et receptissimi prophetae David. Ille apud nos canit Christum, per quem se cecinit ipse Christus. Accipe Christum et audi dominum patri deo colloquentem: Quia tu es qui avulsisti me ex utero matris meae. Eece unum. Et spes mea ab uberibus matris meae, super te sum proiectus ex vulva. Ecce aliud. Et ab utero matris meae deus meus es tu. Ecce aliud. Nunc ad sensus ipsos decertemus. Avulsisti, inquit, ex utero. Quid avellitur, nisi quod inhaeret, quod infixum, innexum est ei a quo ut auferatur avellitur? Si non adhaesit utero, quomodo avulsus est? si adhaesit qui avulsus est, quomodo adhaesisset, nisi dum ex utero est per illum nervum umbilicarem, quasi folliculi sui traducem, adnexus origini vulvae? Etiam cum quid extraneum extraneo adglutinatur, ita concarnatur et convisceratur cum eo cui adglutinatur ut, cum avellitur, rapiat secum ex corpore aliquid a quo avellitur, quasi sequelam quandam abruptae unitatis et traducis mutui coitus. Ceterum quae ubera matris suae nominat? sine dubio quae hausit. Respondeant obstetrices, medici et physici de uberum natura, an aliter manare soleant, sine vulvae genitali passione, pendentibus exinde venis sentinam illam inferni sanguinis in mamillam et ipsa translatione decequentibus in materiam lactis laetiorem. Inde adeo fit ut ubsrum tempore menses sanguinum vacent. Quodsi verbum caro ex se factum est, non ex vulvae communicatione, nihil operata vulva, nihil functa, nihil passa, quomodo fontem suum transfudit in ubera, quae nisi babendo non mutat? Habere autem sanguinem non potuit lacti subministrando, si non haberet causas sanguinis ipsius, avulsionem scilicet suae carnis. Quid fuerit novitatis in Christo ex virgine nascendi palam est, scilicet solumunodo hoc, quod ex virgine, secundum rationem quam edidimus, eo uti virgo esset regeneratio nestra spiritaliter ab omnibus inquinamentis sanctificata per Christum, virginem et ipsum, etiam carnaliter, ut ex virginis carne.
thought_title: The grammar of birth: 'in' and 'from' the virgin
orientation: Tertullian is answering heretics who say Christ was born 'through' or 'in' the virgin but not 'from' her, and he now argues from Scripture and physiology that Christ's flesh truly came from Mary's womb.
pass_a_gloss: But what is your crookedness, that you seek to take away the very syllable EX assigned to the office of a preposition, and to use another more, which in this kind is not found among the holy Scriptures? You say he was born through the virgin, not from the virgin, and in the womb, not from the womb, because also the angel in dreams to Joseph: For that which is born in her, he says, is of the Holy Spirit, he did not say from her. Surely nevertheless, even if he had said from her, he had said in her; for in her was that which was from her. Therefore equally also when he says in her, it agrees with from her, because from her was that which was in her. But it is well that the same Matthew, running down the origin of the Lord from Abraham all the way to Mary, says, Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ is born. But also Paul imposes silence on these grammarians. God, he says, sent his Son made from a woman. Surely not through a woman, or in a woman? This indeed more emphatically, because he says made rather than born; for he would have stated born more simply. But by saying made, he both sealed the saying, The Word was made flesh, and asserted the truth of the flesh made from the virgin. The psalms also will plead for us in this kind, not indeed of the apostate and heretic and Platonic Valentinus, but of the most holy and most received prophet David. He sings among us Christ, through whom Christ himself sang himself. Receive Christ and hear the Lord speaking with the Father God: Because you are he who tore me away from the womb of my mother. Behold one thing. And my hope from the breasts of my mother, upon you I was cast from the womb. Behold another. And from the womb of my mother you are my God. Behold another. Now let us fight it out at the very senses. You tore me away, he says, from the womb. What is torn away, except that which clings, which is fixed, fastened to that from which it is torn away so that it may be removed? If he did not cling to the womb, how was he torn away? If he who was torn away clung, how would he have clung, except while he is from the womb through that umbilical cord, as a shoot of his own little sac, attached to the origin of the womb? Even when something foreign is glued to something foreign, it is so made one in flesh and one in inward parts with that to which it is glued that, when it is torn away, it snatches with itself something from the body from which it is torn away, as a certain sequel of the broken unity and of the mutual joining of the shoot. But what breasts of his mother does he name? Without doubt those which he drank. Let the midwives, doctors and natural philosophers answer about the nature of the breasts, whether they are accustomed to flow otherwise, without the genital passion of the womb, the veins hanging from there straining that bilge of lower blood into the nipple and by that very transfer cooking it into the more pleasant material of milk. From there it comes about that in the time of the breasts the monthly bloods are empty. But if the Word was made flesh from itself, not from the sharing of the womb, the womb having worked nothing, having performed nothing, having suffered nothing, how did it pour its fountain into the breasts, which it does not change except by having? But it could not have blood for supplying milk, if it did not have the causes of that very blood, namely the tearing away of its own flesh. What there was of newness in Christ being born from the virgin is plain, namely only this, that he was from the virgin, according to the reason which we have published, so that the virgin would be our spiritual regeneration, sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself also a virgin, even carnally, as from the flesh of the virgin.

choices.why: The whole section turns on the preposition ex meaning origin or source, not mere location or passage; the glossary requires 'virgin' for virgo.
The heretics' phrase is contrasted with ex vulva; 'womb' is the glossary term for uterus/vulva.
Tertullian stresses factum ('made') over natum ('born') to link with 'the Word was made flesh'; 'from a woman' keeps the source force of ex.

choices.english: you tore me away from the womb
choices.why: The verb avello means violent tearing away, which Tertullian exploits to prove physical attachment; 'womb' is the glossary term.
rejected: you drew me out of the womb
you pulled me from the womb

choices.why: Tertullian uses nervus for the cord connecting fetus to womb; 'umbilical cord' is the standard anatomical rendering.
Sentina is bilge-water, a vivid metaphor for menstrual blood; 'lower blood' keeps the spatial sense of inferni without modernizing.
rejected: that dregs of the blood below

pass_b_english: But how crooked you are! You try to take away the very syllable EX, which is assigned the function of a preposition, and use another one instead, which in this kind of expression is not found in the holy Scriptures. You say he was born through the virgin, not from the virgin, and in the womb, not from the womb, because the angel in a dream said to Joseph: “For what is born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20), not “from her.” Yet surely, even if he had said “from her,” he had said “in her”; for what was from her was in her. So when he says “in her,” it agrees with “from her,” because what was in her was from her. But it is good that the same Matthew, tracing the origin of the Lord from Abraham down to Mary, says: “Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ is born” (Matthew 1:16). Paul also silences these grammarians. “God,” he says, “sent his Son made from a woman” (Galatians 4:4). Is it “through a woman” or “in a woman”? This is even more emphatic, because he says “made” rather than “born”; he could have said “born” more simply. But by saying “made,” he also confirmed “the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14) and asserted the truth of the flesh made from the virgin. The Psalms will also support us in this matter—not the Psalms of the apostate and heretic and Platonist Valentinus, but of the most holy and most received prophet David. He sings among us of Christ, through whom Christ himself sang of himself. Take Christ and hear the Lord speaking to God the Father: “Because you are the one who tore me away from my mother’s womb” (Psalm 22:9). There is one. “And my hope from my mother’s breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb” (Psalm 22:10). There is another. “And from my mother’s womb you are my God” (Psalm 22:10). There is another. Now let us contend with the senses themselves. “You tore me away,” he says, “from the womb.” What is torn away except what clings, what is fixed, what is fastened to that from which it is torn away so that it may be removed? If he did not cling to the womb, how was he torn away? If he who was torn away clung, how would he have clung except by being from the womb through that umbilical cord, like the channel of its own sac, attached to the origin of the womb? Even when something foreign is glued to something foreign, it is so made one in flesh and one in inward parts with that to which it is glued that, when it is torn away, it carries with it something from the body from which it is torn away, like a kind of sequel of the broken unity and of the channel of mutual union. Besides, what breasts of his mother does he name? Without doubt the ones from which he drank. Let midwives, doctors, and natural philosophers answer about the nature of breasts: do they not usually flow only when the womb undergoes its generative disturbance, the veins hanging from there drawing that residue of lower blood into the nipple and by that very transfer transforming it into the sweeter material of milk? That is why during the time of breastfeeding the monthly bloods are absent. But if the Word was made flesh from himself, not from sharing in the womb—the womb doing nothing, performing nothing, suffering nothing—how did the womb pour its fountain into the breasts, which it does not change except by having it? But it could not have blood to supply milk if it did not have the causes of that blood, namely the tearing away of its own flesh. What was new in Christ being born from the virgin is plain: only this, that he was from the virgin, according to the reasoning we have given, so that our regeneration might be a virgin, spiritually sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself a virgin, and also carnally, as from the flesh of a virgin.

problems.quote: so that our regeneration might be spiritual, a virgin sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself a virgin also in the flesh, as from the flesh of a virgin.
problems.source_quote: eo uti virgo esset regeneratio nestra spiritaliter ab omnibus inquinamentis sanctificata per Christum, virginem et ipsum, etiam carnaliter, ut ex virginis carne.
problems.why: Latin says regeneration should be a virgin both spiritually and carnally; English drops 'both' and garbles the parallel.
problems.fix: so that our regeneration might be a virgin, spiritually sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself a virgin, and also carnally, as from the flesh of a virgin.
problems.ruling: Latin 'virgo esset regeneratio nostra spiritaliter ... etiam carnaliter' says regeneration is a virgin both spiritually and carnally; English renders only spiritual and drops 'both' and the metaphor.

edits.old: so that our regeneration might be spiritual, a virgin sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself a virgin also in the flesh, as from the flesh of a virgin.
edits.new: so that our regeneration might be a virgin, spiritually sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself a virgin, and also carnally, as from the flesh of a virgin.

fixed: The English dropped the parallel 'both spiritually and carnally' and garbled the syntax; the source says regeneration should be a virgin both spiritually and carnally, so the edit restores the parallel.

problems.quote: like a shoot of its own little sac
problems.why: Traducem here means 'conduit/channel', not 'shoot'; folliculi is 'sac/pouch', not 'little sac'
problems.fix: like the channel of its own sac
problems.ruling: Latin traducem = conduit/channel, not “shoot”; translation mis‑renders key metaphor.

problems.quote: like a kind of sequel of the broken unity and of the mutual shoot of union
problems.source_quote: quasi sequelam quandam abruptae unitatis et traducis mutui coitus
problems.fix: like a kind of sequel of the broken unity and of the channel of mutual union
problems.ruling: Traducis = of the conduit, coitus = joining; translation “shoot of union” distorts meaning.

problems.quote: so that our regeneration might be a virgin, spiritually sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself a virgin, and also carnally, as from the flesh of a virgin
problems.source_quote: eo uti virgo esset regeneratio nestra spiritaliter ab omnibus inquinamentis sanctificata per Christum, virginem et ipsum, etiam carnaliter, ut ex virginis carne
problems.why: Nestram = nostram; 'might be a virgin' misses 'might use the virgin'; etiam carnaliter modifies sanctified
problems.fix: so that our regeneration might use the virgin, spiritually sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself a virgin, and also carnally, as from the flesh of a virgin
problems.ruling: Latin says “that the virgin might be our regeneration… virginem et ipsum…”, not “our regeneration might be a virgin”; translation reverses subject and omits elements.

problems.quote: which he does not change unless by having?
problems.why: Latin says the breasts do not change except by suckling (babendo), not "unless by having".
problems.fix: which does not change except by suckling
problems.ruling: babendo means 'by suckling/nursing,' not 'by having'; translation loses the specific breastfeeding context central to the argument.

traducis means channel/conduit; coitus means joining/union, not shoot of union
source has 'eo uti virgo esset regeneratio nostra' - 'might use the virgin', not 'might be a virgin'

problems.why: Tertullian uses 'flesh' (caro) and 'body' (corpus) technically distinct but often interchangeably; reader cannot track when distinction matters.
problems.fix: Note when 'body' means soma/corpus vs. when 'flesh' means sarx/caro.

problems.quote: what breasts of his mother does he name? Without doubt the ones he drank from
problems.why: Rhetorical question with abrupt answer; 'he' refers to Christ in Psalm, but shifts to David/Christ ambiguously.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'The Psalmist (Christ speaking) names the breasts he drank from.'

problems.why: 'Bilge' is nautical term for dirty water; applied to maternal blood is graphic but possibly too crude.
problems.fix: Use 'residue' or 'sump' if technical, or keep with note.

problems.quote: cooking it into the sweeter material of milk
problems.why: 'Cooking' is literal translation of coquere but reads as odd metaphor for physiological process.

problems.quote: Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Christ is born
problems.why: Matthew 1:16; but Greek has 'from whom was born Jesus' (feminine, referring to Mary). Tertullian's 'from whom' could read as masculine (Joseph).

edits.old: cooking it into the sweeter material of milk
edits.new: transforming it into the sweeter material of milk

edits.old: Besides, what breasts of his mother does he name? Without doubt the ones he drank from.
edits.new: Besides, what breasts of his mother does he name? Without doubt the ones from which he drank.

fixed: Glossary note about flesh/body: no edit needed; the English consistently uses 'flesh' for caro and 'body' for corpus, and the brief's glossary already covers caro.
Unreadable rhetorical question: clarified 'the ones he drank from' to 'the ones from which he drank' to make the antecedent unambiguous without adding a gloss.
Mistranslation 'bilge': changed to 'residue' to avoid the nautical connotation while keeping the sense of sentinam as dregs or residue.
Mistranslation 'cooking': changed to 'transforming' to render decoquentibus naturally in a physiological context.
Wrong scripture Matthew 1:16: no edit needed; the English follows Tertullian's Latin 'ex qua nascitur Christus', and the ambiguity is in the source, not the translation.

problems.quote: so that our regeneration might use the virgin
problems.source_quote: eo uti virgo esset regeneratio nestra spiritaliter ab omnibus inquinamentis sanctificata per Christum
problems.why: 'eo uti' is a purpose clause (so that), not the verb 'use'. The sense is that our regeneration might itself be a virgin, sanctified from all defilements. The English invents an object.
problems.fix: so that our regeneration might be a virgin, spiritually sanctified from all defilements through Christ, himself a virgin, also in the flesh, as being from a virgin's flesh.

problems.quote: how did he pour his fountain into the breasts
problems.source_quote: quomodo fontem suum transfudit in ubera
problems.why: After the womb has done nothing, the womb—not the Word—pours her fountain into the breasts.
problems.fix: how did the womb pour her own fountain into the breasts
problems.ruling: Subject of 'transfudit' is the vulva ('nihil operata vulva… quomodo fontem suum transfudit'); fontem suum is the womb's blood, not the Word's, so 'he' misattributes agency.

problems.quote: which does not change except by suckling
problems.why: babendo is habendo: the womb does not change the blood except by having it, not by suckling.
problems.fix: she who does not change it except by having it
problems.ruling: 'babendo' is clearly 'habendo' (cf. next sentence 'Habere autem sanguinem'); 'only by having it' was meant, so 'by suckling' invents a different claim.

problems.quote: But he could not have blood to supply milk if he did not have the causes of that blood, namely the tearing away of his own flesh.
problems.source_quote: Habere autem sanguinem non potuit lacti subministrando, si non haberet causas sanguinis ipsius, avulsionem scilicet suae carnis.
problems.why: The womb could not supply milk’s blood without the tearing away of her own flesh.
problems.fix: But the womb could not have had blood to supply the milk unless it had the causes of that blood, namely the tearing away of its own flesh.
problems.ruling: Continues the womb's subject: 'Habere sanguinem non potuit… causas sanguinis ipsius, avulsionem suae carnis' means the womb's own flesh, not Christ's; 'he' wrongly shifts agency.

edits.old: so that our regeneration might use the virgin, spiritually sanctified from all defilements through Christ
edits.new: so that our regeneration might be a virgin, spiritually sanctified from all defilements through Christ

edits.old: how did he pour his fountain into the breasts, which does not change except by suckling?
edits.new: how did the womb pour its fountain into the breasts, which it does not change except by having it?

edits.old: But he could not have blood to supply milk if he did not have the causes of that blood, namely the tearing away of his own flesh.
edits.new: But it could not have blood to supply milk if it did not have the causes of that blood, namely the tearing away of its own flesh.

fixed: 'eo uti virgo esset regeneratio nostra': purpose clause meaning our regeneration might itself be a virgin; fixed 'use the virgin' to 'be a virgin'.
'quomodo fontem suum transfudit in ubera' with 'nihil operata vulva': subject is the womb, fixed 'he poured his' to 'the womb pour its'.
'quae nisi habendo non mutat': habendo means by having, not suckling; fixed 'except by suckling' to 'except by having it'.
'Habere autem sanguinem non potuit ... avulsionem scilicet suae carnis': subject is the womb and suae is the womb's; fixed 'he/his own flesh' to 'it/its own flesh'.

last_rejected.quote: “God,” he says, “sent his Son made from a woman” (Galatians 4:4)

last_rejected.fix: Cite the correct wording “born of a woman” or adjust citation.

last_rejected.quote: through whom Christ himself sang of himself
last_rejected.source_quote: Ille apud nos canit Christum, per quem se cecinit ipse Christus
last_rejected.why: per quem refers to David: Christ sang of himself through David, not through Christ.
last_rejected.fix: He sings among us of Christ, and through him Christ himself sang of himself.
last_rejected.ruling: 'per quem' has Christum as nearest antecedent; the English keeps the Latin's ambiguity. It is awkward but within range, though 'through him' would be clearer.

last_rejected.quote: And my hope from my mother’s breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb” (Psalm 22:10)
last_rejected.source_quote: Et spes mea ab uberibus matris meae, super te sum proiectus ex vulva

last_rejected.fix: “And my hope from my mother’s breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb” (Psalm 22:9–10).
last_rejected.ruling: The quotation spans Psalm 22:9–10: 'spes mea ab uberibus' is verse 9, 'proiectus ex vulva' is verse 10. Citing 22:10 is a minor imprecision, not a changed meaning.

last_rejected.quote: himself a virgin, and also carnally, as from the flesh of a virgin

last_rejected.why: etiam carnaliter modifies Christ as virgin, not our regeneration as also carnal.
